item.title: Judge temporarily blocks deportation of Nigerian national
item.description: The High Court in Suva has temporarily stopped the deportation of Nigerian national Tagbo Nonso Sylvester while it considers his legal challenge against decisions by Fiji’s immigration authorities to refuse him a student visa and order his removal from the country. Sylvester had arrived in Fiji to study at Fiji National University.
item.content:encoded:
The High Court in Suva has temporarily stopped the deportation of Nigerian national Tagbo Nonso Sylvester while it considers his legal challenge against decisions by Fiji’s immigration authorities to refuse him a student visa and order his removal from the country.

Sylvester had arrived in Fiji to study at Fiji National University.

Justice Usaia Ratuvili, in a ruling delivered on August 7, granted Sylvester leave to pursue judicial review and issued an interim stay preventing his deportation until August 12.

The State challenges decisions made on May 20 and July 27 to initially refuse Sylvester a student visa, reject his subsequent appeal and order his deportation from Fiji.

Justice Ratuvili said the central issue raised by the judicial review application was whether the decisions had been made in a procedurally fair manner and whether Sylvester had been accorded natural justice.

The court noted that Sylvester had been given 14 days’ notice of deportation and considered the consequences of removing him while his legal challenge remained unresolved.

“There is no doubt that Tagbo Nonso Sylvester has an interest in the outcome of these proceedings,” Justice Ratuvili said.

“He has been given 14 days’ notice of deportation and there is a certainty that this matter will remain unresolved in his absence.”

However, the judge also acknowledged the State’s authority over immigration matters.

“Balanced against that is the sovereign right of the Republic of Fiji to decide who is entitled to enter and reside within its borders,” he said.

Justice Ratuvili said the competing considerations required the court to determine where the balance of convenience lay.

“This raises the question of where the balance of convenience lies, and in looking at the application as a whole, I find it appropriate to grant an interim stay against deportation until the Respondents are present and we can review that order,” he ruled.

The court granted Sylvester leave to proceed with the judicial review and directed that all respondents be served with the documents filed in the proceedings.

The interim stay on Sylvester’s deportation was ordered to remain valid until Wednesday, August 12, when all parties were required to appear before the High Court for a review of the stay and further directions.

item.title: Very dry conditions forecast across Fiji as El Niño continues
item.description: Very dry conditions are expected across large parts of Fiji in the coming weeks and months as El Niño conditions continue, according to the Fiji Meteorological Service’s Early Action Rainfall Watch. The latest outlook indicates a high chance of very dry conditions across several parts of the country between August 15 and 28.
item.content:encoded:
Very dry conditions are expected across large parts of Fiji in the coming weeks and months as El Niño conditions continue, according to the Fiji Meteorological Service’s Early Action Rainfall Watch.

The latest outlook indicates a high chance of very dry conditions across several parts of the country between August 15 and 28.

Areas facing a high chance of very dry conditions include the Northern Division, Yasawa Group, Viwa, the Nausori to Navua corridor, eastern interior of Viti Levu, northern Kadavu, Moala, Totoya, the Lau Group and Rotuma.

The rest of the Fiji Group has a medium chance of experiencing very dry conditions during the same period.

The outlook for August indicates an even greater risk for some areas.

Rotuma faces a very high chance of very dry conditions, while parts of the southern Lau Group have a high chance.

The Western, Central and Northern divisions, Lomaiviti Group, Moala Group and northern Lau Group have a medium chance of very dry conditions during August.

The outlook becomes more widespread over the August to October period.

The Fiji Meteorological Service says there is a very high chance of very dry conditions for the southern Yasawa Group, Viwa, Mamanuca Group, the Ba to Nadi coastal area, Udu Point, Rabi, Qamea, Gau, Nairai, the Moala Group, Lau Group and Rotuma.

The remainder of Fiji faces a high chance of very dry conditions during the three-month period.

The outlook comes as El Niño is currently underway.

The Early Action Rainfall Watch is designed to provide the Fiji National Disaster Risk Management Office and other disaster management agencies with information on recent rainfall patterns and expected rainfall conditions for the coming months.

The outlook provides authorities with advance information to support preparedness and early action as dry conditions develop across the country.

item.title: Sayed-Khaiyum warns against conflating qoliqoli rights with Marine Areas Bill
item.description: Former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum has urged lawmakers and stakeholders not to conflate traditional qoliqoli fishing rights with the Commercial Use of Marine Areas Bill, saying the two issues need to be considered separately. Sayed-Khaiyum made the comments today before the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights during its consideration of the Commercial Use of Marine Areas B
item.content:encoded:
Former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum has urged lawmakers and stakeholders not to conflate traditional qoliqoli fishing rights with the Commercial Use of Marine Areas Bill, saying the two issues need to be considered separately.

Sayed-Khaiyum made the comments today before the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights during its consideration of the Commercial Use of Marine Areas Bill (Bill No. 42 of 2025).

He rejected suggestions that opposition to the Bill would amount to opposition to qoliqoli rights.

“Let’s not try and conflict the issue. Nor should we try and obfuscate the issue,” Sayed-Khaiyum said.»

“Saying, ‘Oh, anybody opposing this Bill means they don’t believe in qoliqoli rights.’ That’s nonsense. That’s nonsennonsense.”

He said qoliqoli rights are already recognised under the Fisheries Act and need to be properly enforced in areas where they apply.

Sayed-Khaiyum said there were also examples of goli goli owners reaching arrangements with tourism operators that provided financial benefits through mechanisms such as profit sharing and compensation.

He said the question of compensation could become more complicated in areas where fishing resources had been depleted.

“One particular revenue in government, one of the landowners said, ‘We actually no longer—there’s no fish here. We actually can’t fish. There’s nothing here now.’”

Sayed-Khaiyum said this raised the question of how much compensation, if any, should be provided, with such matters potentially being subject to negotiation.

He also cautioned against arrangements that provide immediate lump-sum payments without considering the long-term interests of younger generations.

“Sometimes we’ve seen in some places where goli goli owners demand a lump sum. Just give us half a million dollars now,” he said.

While acknowledging that landowners may receive a substantial payment, Sayed-Khaiyum questioned the impact of permanently giving up a particular fishing right.

“How is it going to affect the young kids who suddenly will become adults who want to fish? You’ve given away that particular right.”

He said a long-term approach was needed, particularly because the benefits and consequences of decisions made today could extend to future generations.

Sayed-Khaiyum also described the relationship between landowners and tourism operators as potentially “symbiotic”, saying successful commercial developments could increase the value of surrounding land and create further economic opportunities.

He said the issue should therefore not be viewed simply as a one-off transaction, but in terms of sustainable and long-term benefits for communities and future generations.

item.title: Suva City Council ordered to pay vendor $40,000 pending appeal
item.description: The Fiji Court of Appeal has ordered the Suva City Council to make a $40,000 interim payment to market vendor Krishan Kumar while the Council’s appeal against a $132,591 damages award remains pending. Resident Justice of Appeal Chandana Prematilaka made the order on August 3 after considering competing applications from Kumar and the Council arising from a High Court judgment.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Court of Appeal has ordered the Suva City Council to make a $40,000 interim payment to market vendor Krishan Kumar while the Council’s appeal against a $132,591 damages award remains pending.

Resident Justice of Appeal Chandana Prematilaka made the order on August 3 after considering competing applications from Kumar and the Council arising from a High Court judgment.

Kumar had successfully sued the Council after claiming he fell at the Suva Market when a rope tied between a tarpaulin and a market stall caught his left foot.

He suffered injuries in the fall and sought damages for pain and suffering, economic loss, future care and other expenses.

The Council had denied liability, maintaining that its staff regularly inspected the market and had not seen a rope obstructing the walkway. It also argued that Kumar had failed to keep a proper lookout.

The High Court, however, found that the Council owed Kumar a duty of care and had breached that duty. It also rejected the Council’s claim of contributory negligence.

Kumar was awarded a total of $132,591.15, including $60,000 in general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenities, $52,000 for loss of future earnings and additional amounts for care, medical and travel expenses, interest and costs.

The Council subsequently appealed the decision and sought a stay preventing enforcement of the judgment.

Justice Prematilaka found that the appeal raised arguable issues and should not be dismissed at this stage.

“The appellant appears to have an arguable case with regard to other damages in appeal and the quantum in general damages as well,” Justice Prematilaka said.

“This also means that the appeal is not vexatious or frivolous and should not be dismissed at this stage.”

However, the judge noted that the appeal could take considerable time to reach a full hearing because the judge’s notes and transcript had not yet been received.

“Therefore, considering all circumstances I am inclined to allow an interim payment of $40,000.00 to be paid by the appellant to the respondent pending appeal,” Justice Prematilaka ruled.

The Court also rejected the Council’s application for a stay of execution.

Justice Prematilaka said that in money judgments, a successful litigant should generally not be prevented from receiving the benefit of a judgment simply because an appeal was pending.

“In the case of money judgments, generally a successful litigant should not be deprived of the fruits of successful litigation by withholding funds to which he is otherwise entitled, pending an appeal,” he said.

The judge ultimately found the Council’s stay application was premature and declined to grant it.

The Court ordered the Suva City Council to pay Kumar $40,000 plus prescribed post-judgment interest within 21 days.

It also ordered the Council to pay Kumar $2,500 in costs within 21 days.

Kumar’s application to have the Council’s appeal dismissed was refused, meaning the substantive appeal against the High Court judgment will continue.

item.title: Two-thirds of Fijians without mobile phones rely on someone else’s device
item.description: More than two-thirds of Fijians who do not personally own a mobile phone regularly use someone else’s device, highlighting the importance of phone sharing in maintaining access to communication and digital services. The Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025 found that 68 per cent of non-mobile phone owners regularly use another person’s mobile phone or SIM.
item.content:encoded:
More than two-thirds of Fijians who do not personally own a mobile phone regularly use someone else’s device, highlighting the importance of phone sharing in maintaining access to communication and digital services.

The Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025 found that 68 per cent of non-mobile phone owners regularly use another person’s mobile phone or SIM.

The practice is particularly common among women and younger Fijians.

According to the survey, 74 per cent of women without their own mobile phone regularly use someone else’s device, compared with 60 per cent of men.

The rate was also 74 per cent among people aged 15 to 35, compared with 61 per cent among those aged 36 to 55 and 69 per cent for the 56 to 65 age group.

Among those aged 66 and above, 54 per cent regularly relied on another person’s phone.

The survey also reveals a significant rural-urban difference, with 72 per cent of rural non-phone owners using someone else’s device compared with 62 per cent in urban areas.

It suggests the higher levels of sharing among women, young people and rural residents may indicate a greater need for mobile phones among these groups.

Making calls or sending messages was by far the most common reason for sharing a device, cited by 76 per cent of respondents.

About 51 per cent used another person’s phone to access the internet, while smaller proportions used shared devices to receive money, send money, make payments, access mobile money accounts, buy airtime or for entertainment.

The survey found women were slightly more likely than men to share a phone to access the internet, make payments or send and receive money.

Among Fijians who did not own a mobile phone, 14 per cent reported using another person’s device to make a payment, while seven per cent did so regularly.

item.title: Two charged with murder over death of Vimal Nand
item.description: Two men have been charged with murder following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand after an alleged assault in Sigatoka over the weekend. Police confirmed the two accused, aged 19 and 51, will be produced at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday, August 13.
item.content:encoded:
Two men have been charged with murder following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand after an alleged assault in Sigatoka over the weekend.

Police confirmed the two accused, aged 19 and 51, will be produced at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday, August 13.

The pair have been jointly charged with one count of murder, one count of act with intent to cause grievous harm and one count of assault causing actual bodily harm.

The charges follow an alleged confrontation involving Nand, his son and another student while they were out horse riding.

According to police, the two suspects allegedly confronted the three over the weekend.

Nand was later found unconscious by his brother with serious head injuries.

He was initially taken to Sigatoka Hospital before being transferred to Nadi Hospital and subsequently to Lautoka Hospital because of the seriousness of his injuries.

Nand later died at Lautoka Hospital despite attempts to revive him.

The two accused are expected to make their first court appearance on the charges at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday.

item.title: Classify security services as essential, says Nand
item.description: SECURITY services must be formally classified as an essential service alongside the police force to ensure guards receive proper professional recognition and resources, says Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand. Making the plea during the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 yesterday, Mr Nand said that private guards were consistent
item.content:encoded:
SECURITY services must be formally classified as an essential service alongside the police force to ensure guards receive proper professional recognition and resources, says Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand.

Making the plea during the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 yesterday, Mr Nand said that private guards were consistently on the front lines during major crises.

“COVID is there, natural disasters is there, everything is there. Our guards are still at the sites. We are still in the field,” he said.

During strict movement curfews, Mr Nand said officers were required to remain active round-the-clock to check on personnel, monitor client properties, and protect closed premises from looting.

“I think the industry should be an essential service permanently.

“So that we will get the recognition we deserve. And, at the same time, we will also get the perks which come along with it, like the training aspect.”

Mr Nand said many commercial clients failed to prioritise security until after a severe incident occurred.

He said property owners frequently relied on basic measures such as lighting and surveillance equipment, which failed to deter intruders who concealed their identities.

“Thieves nowadays cover themselves from head to toe.

“They look at the camera, they wave at the camera, they break things, they take stuff out, they move and they know they can’t be detected because there is no clue.”

item.title: Calls for major reforms
item.description: Fiji’s private security industry is calling for major reforms to the Security Industry Act 2010, with concerns over worker exploitation, high staff turnover and changing workforce dynamics prompting calls for a modern regulatory framework. The concerns were raised during a public consultation on the review of the Act at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s private security industry is calling for major reforms to the Security Industry Act 2010, with concerns over worker exploitation, high staff turnover and changing workforce dynamics prompting calls for a modern regulatory framework.

The concerns were raised during a public consultation on the review of the Act at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.

Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand said stronger regulation was needed to protect security guards and improve standards across the industry.

He said some non-compliant employers continued to exploit workers by failing to provide basic employment benefits.

“In terms of rights, many of their guards have come running to us,” Mr Nand said.

“They don’t give them FNPF or any leave. Sometimes they even exploit their workers, paying them only partially.”

He said poor working conditions had contributed to high staff turnover, making it increasingly difficult for companies to retain experienced guards.

“We are always looking for guards. This is an industry where the turnover is very high. People just come, and as soon as they get something better, they go.”

Mr Nand also noted a decline in former military and police personnel entering the sector, with more attractive career opportunities drawing experienced workers elsewhere.

The review of the 2010 Act is expected to strengthen industry regulation, improve worker protections and ensure the sector keeps pace with changing workforce needs.

ESCALATING on-the-job risks have sparked urgent calls to allow private security guards to carry batons and handcuffs, following public consultations yesterday on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 in Lautoka.

Speaking after session proceedings at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom, Commissioner for the review of the Act Ana Rokomokoti emphasised that evolving workplace dangers necessitate stronger protective measures for frontline personnel.

“The idea is to give them an opportunity to be able to defend themselves, considering that the security environment nowadays is very different from what it was ten years ago,” she said.

“The risks are higher and there’s more exposure to such risks.”

Ms Rokomokoti said that 16 years have passed since the original legislation was enacted, making the current review critical to addressing modern operational realities but she stressed that updating the legal framework required direct feedback from those working within the industry.

“A lot has changed in the security landscape, and this review is very timely, but the review cannot be successful without the input from the members of the public.

“I’d really plead with especially those who are involved in the security business to come forward and give us their views.” Professional Security Services Ltd regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand pointed out that the lack of restraint equipment posed severe safety hazards for officers handling volatile individuals

A VAST majority of security company employees and employers are calling for the implementing of 12-hour shifts particularly for those looking to make more income for their families.

This was highlighted during a public consultation on the review of the Security Act 2010 held at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.

Speaking at the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010,

Commissioner for Ana Rokomokoti said this was also highlighted during the initial consultation in Suva on Monday.

“There was a good turnout in Suva, there was a lot of emphasis on the shift, from 8 hours to 12 hours but of course, I accept that the propositions coming from employer’s perspective,” she said.

“There is a suggestion that the 12-hour shift is something that the government should consider shifting towards and they gave the pros and cons.”

Ms Rokomokoti said many employees were focused on the take homer salary at the end of the week, particularly for security guards who were also sole breadwinners for their families.

“I think we had the figures from $227 or $220 to $331 per week net (if approved ).” Ms Rokomokoti said this suggestion seemed to be one agreed upon by both employers and employees, but the committee would also need to sort through the written submissions made via email.
